source: Wong, Collins, Ying, Zhang, Weller, Gerstenberg, O'Donnell, Lew, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Brooke-Wilson (2025) Modeling open-world cognition as on-demand synthesis of probabilistic models
finding: Gap 2 and 4. The paper compares the model-synthesis architecture (MSA) with Llama-3.1-70B direct and chain-of-thought (CoT) baselines, but reports no token counts, latency or compute-matched comparison. R2 values for the LM baselines appear only as heatmap colours and scatterplots, not in text.
numbers: Participants: Exp1 N=78, Exp2 N=80, Exp3 N=20 (plus 20 for elicitation). MSA: 10 simulated participants per vignette, 1000 samples (Exp1-2) or 500 (Exp3) of rejection sampling in WebPPL. LM baselines: temperature 1.0, 5 scalar judgments x 8 questions.
quote: as it involves greater computation in language ... but no explicit symbolic model execution
limits: The only cost remark is that rejection sampling 'incurs a significant time cost'. Base LM is Llama-3.1-70B, not a frontier model. Human fit is judged against a split-half human-human 95% CI.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: nobody has shown the translate-then-infer gain survives equal-token CoT.

source: Wong, Collins, Ying, Zhang, Weller, Gerstenberg, O'Donnell, Lew, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Brooke-Wilson (2025) Modeling open-world cognition as on-demand synthesis of probabilistic models
finding: MSA predictions are stable between detailed (Exp1) and under-specified (Exp2) backgrounds. Human-vs-LM and human-vs-MSA R2 are shown only as colour blocks. Text says humans correlate better with themselves and with symbolic models than with LMs, and the LMs correlate with each other.
numbers: MSA Exp1 vs Exp2 self-consistency scatter labels: R2 about 0.96 (tug-of-war), 0.98 (canoe), 0.95 (biathlon), read from garbled figure text, so approximate.
limits: Exact model-human R2 for LM-Direct and LM-CoT not stated in the text. The gap was larger for canoe racing, a sport not in published literature, and smaller for biathlon. Authors suspect LM training-data familiarity helps the LM on tug-of-war.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly open: LM-only R2 cannot be quoted. The contamination hint warns that LM baselines look better on famous tasks.

source: Wong, Collins, Ying, Zhang, Weller, Gerstenberg, O'Donnell, Lew, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Brooke-Wilson (2025) Modeling open-world cognition as on-demand synthesis of probabilistic models
finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the model samples one program per simulated participant, variance of MSA samples is often too low, and the system struggled to invent models for a truly novel sport.
numbers: Exp3 uses 9 vignettes over two sports (tug-of-war and canoe).
limits: Qualitative remarks; no quantitative failure rate in the text read.
agent_relevance: Plan for low sample variance when the agent builds one model and queries it: sample several models or add noise.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Gap 2. Full text searched for token, cost, latency and CoT comparisons. The paper mentions CoT and scratchpads only in its discussion as related ideas. It has no measured cost and no baseline run.
numbers: No numbers: the paper is a proposal with worked examples (searching for token, cost, latency, correlation found nothing of substance).
limits: Confirms the earlier critique line: illustrative only.
agent_relevance: Cost of translate-then-infer is unknown from this source; the 2025 follow-up also does not report it.

source: Loula et al. (2025) Syntactic and semantic control of LLMs via sequential Monte Carlo (ICLR 2025)
finding: Gap 6. Appendix Table 6 (Llama 3.1 8B base, N=5, 10, 50) gives data-science accuracy by particle count. Full SMC beats Full IS at 10 and 50 particles; at 5 particles the gap is small.
numbers: Data science Full SMC vs Full IS: 5 particles 0.224 vs 0.204; 10 particles 0.285 (0.26,0.32) vs 0.223; 50 particles 0.292 (0.25,0.33) vs 0.218. Main Table 2 (Llama 3 70B): base 0.213, Full SMC 0.346 (0.31,0.39) with a second unlabelled row 0.407 (0.36,0.45).
limits: The 0.346 and 0.407 cells could not be assigned to a named setting from the extracted text. Paper says only that data science gains significantly when going from 5 to 10 particles.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 mostly closed: gain at 5 particles is small (CIs overlap), real from 10 particles. Budget at least 10.

source: Loula et al. (2025) appendix A.1 and A.3
finding: Internal inconsistency found. Table 4 (smaller LM, Llama 3.1 8B for data science, N=10) reports Full SMC data science 0.225, while Table 6 (also Llama 3.1 8B, N=10) reports 0.285. Gains are larger for smaller LMs, and Full SMC with the small LM beats the larger base LM in data science. SMC Steering vs Full SMC on text-to-SQL is 0.607 vs 0.620.
numbers: Table 4: base LM data science 0.114. Text-to-SQL with a 1B instruct model: Full SMC 0.348 vs LM 0.224. Compute: DS-1000 ran on 4 H100 GPUs and 64 vCPUs, other domains on one A100.
limits: Two tables disagree for the same setting; cause not explained in the text.
agent_relevance: Treat data-science numbers as uncertain by about 0.06. Control by checker still works with a small model.

source: Li et al. (2024) Automated statistical model discovery with language models (BoxLM)
finding: Gap 7 cause found. In BoxLM the Peregrine dataset is real counts of peregrines in the French Jura, 1964-2003, 40 observations, expert ELPD -142.19. In RefineStat (ICLR 2026) Peregrine is described as simulated population counts over 9 years, expert ELPD -112.60. They are different datasets under one name, so the numbers are not comparable.
numbers: BoxLM Table 1, expert vs BoxLM: Eight schools -30.70 vs -30.42; Dugongs 22.52 vs 23.40; Surgical -40.29 vs -38.03; Peregrine -142.19 vs -173.11 (BoxLM worse). Appendix GPT-4 text variant Peregrine -164.69.
limits: The small differences in Surgical (-40.29 vs -39.73) and Dugongs (22.52 vs 22.43) look like reruns or different PosteriorDB versions; not explained in the text.
agent_relevance: Do not compare expert baselines across papers. Re-run the expert program.

source: Ghosh et al. (2025) RefineStat: language-model-driven statistical model synthesis (ICLR 2026 oral)
finding: Gap 7. On a fixed set of expert Stan programs from PosteriorDB, OpenAI o3 (a frontier reasoning model) matches the expert on three of five datasets and falls behind on two.
numbers: ELPD-LOO, expert vs o3: Eight schools -30.70 vs -30.74 (sd 0.07); Dugongs 22.43 vs 22.83 (sd 8.12); Surgical -39.73 vs -38.73 (sd 0.51); Peregrine -112.60 vs -133.29 (sd 10.33); GP -26.53 vs -34.95 (sd 13.28). RefineStat with DQ-7B: Eight schools -30.68, Dugongs 8.35, Surgical -114.29, GP -23.39.
limits: Table 3 column layout is garbled in extraction; the DQ-7B Peregrine cell is unclear. These are well-known PosteriorDB models and may be in training data.
agent_relevance: A frontier model without a scaffold already writes a competent probabilistic model on textbook problems, so the scaffold gain is mainly for small models and unfamiliar tasks.

source: Domke (2025) Large Language Bayes
finding: Gap 1 and 2. The method samples 1024 Stan models from Llama-3.3-70B and averages their posteriors. Experiments are qualitative plots on new problems; no CoT or direct-LLM baseline and no accuracy table.
numbers: 1024 models took 10 to 15 minutes on one A100 (4-bit AWQ). The author asks that future work not reuse these problems for LLMs with a cutoff after 21 April 2025.
limits: No quantitative score against any baseline. Marginal likelihoods are estimated, so good models may get lower weights than they deserve.
agent_relevance: Cost anchor for gap 2: about 1000 model generations is minutes of GPU time, but nobody matched it to a CoT budget.

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over uncertain text by generative LLMs (BLInD)
finding: Gap 1. The nearest test of LLM-writes-program-plus-solver against CoT on a non-human-fit task. On Bayesian-network questions (900 test instances) CoT collapses as networks grow, while LLM-written ProbLog or Monte Carlo code stays high.
numbers: GPT-4 few-shot CoT accuracy by number of variables V2..V10: 78, 64, 36, 25, 22, 16, 7, 7, 7 percent. GPT-4 ProbLog: 99, 98, 100, 100, 96, 97, 97, 98, 96. GPT-4 Monte Carlo: 100, 99, 98, 100, 92, 94, 92, 90, 88. GPT-4 plain Python (PAL) falls to 7 at V10.
limits: Models are GPT-3.5, Llama 3 and GPT-4 (2023-24), not reasoning models. Answer counted correct within a tolerance. Translating text to a graph is easy here.
agent_relevance: Strong sign that an external solver wins when exact arithmetic over many variables is needed. Not a test against long CoT from a reasoning model.

source: Nafar et al. (2024) BLInD, CLADDER adaptation and cost remark
finding: Gap 2. On the CLADDER adaptation (100 sampled instances) CoT few-shot with GPT-4 is already 96 percent and PAL 98, so the solver advantage disappears on small natural-language problems. On cost, the authors say CoT adds tokens, while program methods have the same code-generation time as CoT plus milliseconds of solver time.
numbers: CLADDER adaptation, GPT-4: Basic QA zero-shot 20, CoT zero-shot 64, CoT few-shot 96, PAL 98, PAL with number extraction 97, Monte Carlo 97. GPT-3.5: CoT few-shot 26, PAL 75. Llama 3: CoT few-shot 91, PAL 96 (table rows partly scrambled in extraction).
limits: Only 100 items. No token-count table; the cost statement is prose.
agent_relevance: For small problems CoT suffices. Gate the probabilistic route by problem size (many interacting variables).

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships: asking questions in Battleship with language-informed program sampling (CogSci 2024)
finding: Gap 3. Best-of-k by expected information gain was tested up to k=50, with CodeLlama-7b and gpt-4-0613 only. EIG rises with k and passes the human mean at k=10, but never reaches the best human questions. No cost curve and no frontier or reasoning model.
numbers: k=1 mean EIG: CodeLlama 0.65, GPT-4 0.66, grammar 0.36. At k=10 both LLMs beat the human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4 textual few-shot). 88 percent of GPT-4 and 75 percent of CodeLlama samples translated to valid programs. Textual board beat no-board for k=1-20 (p<0.05); visual board (GPT-4V) was no better than no-board for k=10-50.
limits: Single task (single-turn Battleship questions). Model versions are from 2023.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: holds to k=50 for 2023 models; frontier and cost curve remain unknown. Gains flatten, so k about 10 to 20 is a practical choice.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 9. LLM-proposed natural-language hypotheses, then program implementation and checking against training pairs, help on ARC but stay far below solved. It is the closest test of the hypothesis-proposal idea outside the Number Game.
numbers: GPT-4 on a random 100 of 400 ARC training tasks: direct 17 percent, program only 23, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30, human-selected hypotheses 33, human-written hypotheses 45. 1D-ARC (108 tasks): direct 39.6, program only 61.1, full 73.1.
limits: 100-task subset, GPT-4, pre-reasoning-model era. Not a probabilistic program: a pass-all-training-pairs filter replaces Bayesian reweighting.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: propose-then-verify transfers to ARC with a real but limited gain; the Bayesian part is untested there.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Gap 9 and recheck of K14. Online SMC over LLM-proposed rules beats batch and ReAct on Zendo and ActiveACRE, but only on two rule-learning games. No ARC. Authors say hypotheses are simple and stereotyped and abduction of unseen objects is missing.
numbers: Zendo score out of 8: human 5.26, ReAct 4.60, batch fuzzy 5.35, online fuzzy about 6.0, hard-rule variants up to 6.55. Human-fit R2: online fuzzy 0.57, hard rules 0.10, batch 0.05, ReAct 0.25; all single judgments R2 0.35. ActiveACRE task solving: 0.00 for ReAct and fuzzy rules, 0.10 to 0.15 for batch and refinement, 0.35 for online hard rules.
limits: Table row labels are scrambled in the extracted text, so row-to-method mapping of Zendo scores is approximate. Very small hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no evidence beyond rule games from this group.

source: Marcus and Davis (2013) How robust are probabilistic models of higher-level cognition? Psychological Science
finding: Gap 8. A re-examination of Frank and Goodman 2012: the near-perfect fit depends on a post hoc decision rule. With listeners and speakers both winner-take-all (the decision-theoretic standard), or a mixed rule, fits are dramatically poorer in their Figure 4.
numbers: Frank and Goodman bets over 3 objects: fit near perfect with the proportional rule; the same data under two alternative rules give visibly worse curves (shown in a figure, no R2).
limits: Fit differences shown in figures only. A critique with re-analysis of published data, not new data. Goodman and Hamrick (2015) replied and Marcus and Davis answered in 2015; the reply PDF could not be opened (403).
agent_relevance: Fix the decision rule and priors before looking at fit. Supports a guardrail against tuning after the fact.

source: Marcus and Davis (2013), poetry and movie-gross cases
finding: Gap 8. For Griffiths and Tenenbaum 2006 predictions, the authors say the prior and the assumed sampling of questions were chosen post hoc. For movie grosses, a different asking assumption changes the posterior and the conclusion (subjects would then look biased, not optimal).
numbers: Example given: a film with 158 million dollars gross after 3 days contradicts a uniform-over-time prior. Poetry data are compared under two priors in their Fig 2.
limits: Argument by worked example on two tasks; no systematic re-fit across the literature.
agent_relevance: Without independent data on priors, a good fit is weak evidence. Ask where the prior came from before trusting a posterior.

source: Bowers and Davis (2012) Bayesian just-so stories in psychology and neuroscience. Psychological Bulletin 138(3), 389-414
finding: Gap 8. Review of word recognition, motion perception, reasoning and other cases arguing that Bayesian models are flexible enough to explain almost any behavior as optimal, and are seldom compared with non-Bayesian rivals.
numbers: Conceptual review; no pooled statistic or re-analysis.
quote: mathematical analyses of cognition that can be used to explain almost any behavior as optimal
limits: Review, not data. Griffiths et al. dispute the falsifiability claim.
agent_relevance: Run a non-Bayesian rival (a simple heuristic) next to any probabilistic model the agent builds and report both.

source: Griffiths, Chater, Norris, Pouget (2012) How the Bayesians got their beliefs. Psychological Bulletin 138(3), 415-422
finding: Gap 8. The reply: a Bayesian model is an empirical hypothesis that makes testable predictions; flexibility exists in all model families; priors can be measured. Cites Griffiths and Tenenbaum who collected empirical priors and predicted from them. Concedes optimality claims need strong constraints on assumptions.
numbers: No new fit numbers; argument only.
limits: Opinion piece. Bowers and Davis wrote a reply (PDF found, not read).
agent_relevance: Supports the rule: measure the prior independently, then test a new prediction.

source: Waldon and Degen (2021) Modeling cross-linguistic production of referring expressions (SCiL)
finding: Gap 5. This is an RSA extension, not a replication of Frank and Goodman 2012. It needs non-deterministic adjective semantics and incremental utterance choice to explain redundant colour adjectives, which basic RSA does not predict. Authors call English vs Spanish a candidate for cross-linguistic replication studies.
numbers: No fit statistics; model predictions under parameter regimes.
limits: Modelling paper. Searches found no many-labs replication of Frank and Goodman 2012 and none of Lake 2015.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. Treat basic RSA numbers (r=0.98 and 0.99) as one lab, one design.

source: Search-result note: Qing and Franke (2015) close replication of Frank and Goodman 2012, and follow-ups on one-shot web reference games
finding: Search snippets say a close replication exists (Qing and Franke 2015) and that one-shot web-based language games suggest listeners may be less pragmatic than assumed. PDFs could not be downloaded (empty responses), so the text was not read.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Snippet only, not opened. Do not cite for numbers.
agent_relevance: Keep K03 as one-lab evidence until the replication text is read.

source: Pournemat et al. (2025) Reasoning under uncertainty: probabilistic reasoning capabilities of LLMs
finding: Gap 1 background. Direct LLM reasoning over explicit discrete distributions improves with model size but degrades sharply with context length and notation changes. Supports pushing arithmetic over many observations to code.
numbers: Abstract: performance degradation of over 60 percent as context length increases. Tested models include DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and GPT-4o-mini.
limits: Tasks are mode, maximum likelihood and sampling over given distributions, not world-model reasoning.
agent_relevance: Reason for a solver step when evidence tables are long.
